slides.headline: Lore beat slop
slides.aside: the word of the year is lore
slides.body: Sprout Social named “lore” its 2026 social media word of the year: over 10 million mentions, against 8.8 million for “slop”.
slides.take: As the cost of creativity and distribution becomes negligible, the advantage moves to the story itself. Not just telling stories, but telling unique ones in ways that genuinely connect. None of this is new. Storytelling has been ingrained in us for thousands of years; “tell me a story” is the first thing a child asks for at night. The winners of the next decade will be the ones who master the lore.

slides.headline: A meme waited three years
slides.body: Since 2023, a singing polar bear has been reminding people that November 2026 is coming. A version from late August passed 980,000 views in two weeks. Now it's here.
slides.take: We live in an age of instant gratification, where most content is made to be consumed once and forgotten. Building something to be experienced at a future date runs against that grain. It takes foresight and discipline, which is exactly why it cuts through. In a feed of disposable content, patience is becoming one of the few ways left to earn real attention.

slides.headline: Fans paying to watch fans
slides.body: BTS sold 252,000 tickets across three nights in São Paulo, and the cinema livestream made $3M in the US. Their first Brazil fan meeting, in 2014, held 1,500.
slides.take: Live entertainment is turning fan-driven: people want to share the moment with others who feel the same way, an event about the event. Every industry should take note, conferences most of all. Run them in parallel, with smaller rooms in other cities linked live to the main stage, physical and digital at once. Nobody wants to watch a keynote alone at their desk; the whole point is the people. So expand the room, don’t just stream it.

slides.headline: An NBA team will dress as a fake city
slides.body: On 18 Nov, the night before GTA VI launches, the Miami Heat wear “Vice City” jerseys with the GTA VI logo, sold at the arena that day.
slides.take: Brilliant, and a measure of GTA’s cultural weight: a fictional city now carries enough meaning to dress a real team. I’d like to see 2027 bring far more of this, with IP crossing into sport at every level, down to local and private teams, cross-pollinating fan bases that would never otherwise meet.

slides.headline: Harry Styles played his own origin story
slides.body: Closing 30 nights at Madison Square Garden, he dressed as his 2010 X Factor audition self, then as Pizza Rat on Halloween.
slides.take: Audiences don’t fall for music alone. They fall for the person: the story, the history, the point of view. Once fans are devoted, every detail becomes part of a world they’re invested in. The artists who understand that their own story is the deeper product will hold attention long after any single release.

slides.headline: Worlds you can play
slides.body: Genie 4 makes playable, real-time worlds you steer with text, with live sound and dialogue. Trusted testers only for now.
slides.take: The idea that great art and great games won’t survive now that anyone can make anything is a myth. People turn to entertainment to switch off, and to games because the experience is rich and authored. Beyond the novelty, I don’t think generated worlds will hold most people. For aspiring game makers, though, it collapses the distance between an idea and something playable.

slides.headline: Characters that stay the same

media.label: Kling 4.0 · campaign film by UNVEIL · 7 Nov

slides.body: Kling's new model holds a character steady across a 30-second scene, the hurdle that kept these tools from making recurring characters.
slides.take: Character consistency is the last real hurdle. As Ed Catmull put it, it’s just another problem, and every solved problem widens what’s possible. But anyone who has used these tools knows the myth of endless prompted storytelling. Making something that isn’t slop still takes discipline, judgment and an editor’s eye.

slides.headline: Steal the animated story short
slides.body: Its proof is a 67-second short about the 1831 Broughton bridge. Any history story, no filming, no archival footage.
slides.take: I don’t accept the premise that if anyone can make anything, nothing holds value. Access was never the scarce part. Ruthless editing and the discipline to tell one idea coherently are, and they’re about to become some of the most valuable skills in creative work.
